names.primary: Expulsion of the Jews from Spain

location: the Crowns of Castile and Aragon (Spain); the decree issued at Granada

date.note: The Alhambra Decree was signed by the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile, at Granada on 31 March 1492 ('the XXXI day of the month of March, the year ... one thousand four hundred and ninety-two'). It ordered all Jews of Castile and Aragon to depart by the end of July 1492 (the deadline is usually given as 31 July, with the actual last departures in the first days of August).

summary: The Expulsion of the Jews from Spain was ordered by the Alhambra Decree, issued by the Catholic Monarchs Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile at Granada on 31 March 1492, commanding all Jews in the Crowns of Castile and Aragon who would not convert to Christianity to leave the kingdoms by the end of July on pain of death and confiscation of property. It ended one of the oldest and largest Jewish communities in Europe and scattered Sephardic Jewry across the Mediterranean, North Africa, and the Ottoman lands, from which many later reached Safed in the Land of Israel.
description:
The Expulsion of the Jews from Spain was effected by the edict known as the Alhambra Decree, signed by the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile, at Granada on 31 March 1492, months after the fall of Nasrid Granada completed the Christian reconquest of the Iberian peninsula. The decree ordered all Jews of the Crowns of Castile and Aragon, 'those who are natives as those who are not', to depart from the kingdoms by the end of July 1492 and never to return, and it set the penalty for remaining or returning as death and the confiscation of all possessions.

The decree states its own rationale in the monarchs' voice, and this entry reports that stated reason as the text's own attributed justification rather than as neutral fact. The preamble complains that 'there were some wicked Christians who Judaized and apostatized from our holy Catholic faith, the great cause of which was interaction between the Jews and these Christians', that earlier remedies (the segregation of Jews into separate quarters ordered at Toledo in 1480, and the Inquisition established in the years following) had not sufficed, and that so long as Jews remained they would 'subvert and ... steal faithful Christians from our holy Catholic faith'. On that stated ground the monarchs 'resolve to order the said Jews and Jewesses of our kingdoms to depart and never to return'. The decree's own logic thus ties the expulsion of professing Jews to the earlier problem of the conversos, Jews who had converted to Christianity (many under the coercion of the anti-Jewish violence of 1391 and after) and whose sincerity was suspected; the Inquisition, established from 1478 to 1480, existed to police those baptized Christians, whereas the 1492 decree targeted those who still professed Judaism.

In practice the decree left Jews a stark choice: accept baptism and remain, or depart into exile within roughly four months; those who neither converted nor left by the deadline faced the decree's penalties. During the grace period, from 31 March to the end of July, the crown placed the departing Jews under royal safeguard and permitted them to sell and take their movable property, but forbade the export of 'gold or silver or coined money', which sharply reduced what emigrants could carry out of the kingdoms. The number expelled is debated by historians; older estimates ran very high, while more recent scholarship (Kamen) argues for a smaller Jewish population and therefore a lower figure, on the order of tens of thousands, with a substantial further number choosing baptism over exile.

The expulsion ended one of the oldest and largest Jewish communities in Christian Europe and produced the great dispersion of Sephardic Jewry (from Sefarad, the Hebrew name for the Iberian peninsula). Exiles crossed first into neighbouring Portugal (from which they were in turn expelled or forcibly converted in 1497) and Navarre, and spread across the Mediterranean world: to North Africa, to Italy, and above all to the Ottoman Empire, whose sultan is reported to have welcomed the newcomers. Ottoman-ruled cities such as Salonica, Istanbul, and Safed in the Galilee became major centres of Sephardic life; the sixteenth-century flowering of Safed as a centre of Kabbalah and halakha, associated with figures such as Joseph Karo, Moses Cordovero, and Solomon Alkabetz, drew on this Sephardic diaspora. A distinct aftermath was that of the conversos or New Christians (called by their detractors marranos), the baptized descendants of Jews who remained in Iberia, some of whom continued to practise Judaism secretly (crypto-Judaism) and remained subject to the Inquisition for generations. This entry records the decree, its stated rationale, the choice it imposed, the scale and geography of the dispersion, and the converso aftermath as matters of historical record.
editorial_notes:
This entry is grounded in the Alhambra Decree itself, read line-by-line in an open English translation hosted by Florida Atlantic University (the Center for the Study of Human Rights and the Holocaust), which reproduces the full text. The load-bearing facts are taken verbatim from that text: the issuing parties and titles (Ferdinand and Isabella); the stated rationale (that 'wicked Christians who Judaized' were caused by 'interaction between the Jews and these Christians', and that Jews 'subvert and ... steal faithful Christians'); the operative command to 'depart and never to return'; the deadline ('by the end of the month of July'); the death-and-confiscation penalty ('the penalty of death and the confiscation of all their possessions'); the royal safeguard and the ban on exporting 'gold or silver or coined money'; and the dating ('Given in our city of Granada, the XXXI day of the month of March ... one thousand four hundred and ninety-two years'). NEUTRALITY: the decree's stated justification (that Jewish presence subverted Christian converts) is reported strictly as the text's own attributed rationale in the monarchs' voice, not endorsed and not presented as neutral fact about Jews (neutrality #1, #4); the polemical register of the decree ('wicked', 'diabolical astuteness') is quoted as the document's language, never adopted as the entry's own. The number expelled is flagged as debated and attributed to scholarship rather than asserted (neutrality #2, #3).

SOURCING (neutrality #8, #9): (b) PRIMARY, read line-by-line, the Alhambra Decree in open English translation (FAU-hosted), rated high because it was read verbatim and the quoted passages verified against the text. (a) academic historians: Henry Kamen, 'The Mediterranean and the Expulsion of Spanish Jews in 1492', Past & Present 119 (1988), the peer-reviewed study revising the numbers downward, and Benzion Netanyahu, The Origins of the Inquisition in Fifteenth Century Spain (1995), the major (and contested) study of the conversos and the origins of the Inquisition that frames the converso aftermath; both rated medium, verified to exist and be on-topic via the journal and publisher records, not read line-by-line, and Netanyahu's converso thesis is itself a debated scholarly position, cited for the converso context rather than adopted as settled. No encyclopedias, no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources. CONFIDENCE HONESTY: high only on the decree text actually read line-by-line; the numbers, the converso framing, and the diaspora geography rest on secondary scholarship and are rated medium.

relations.note: Many Sephardic exiles of 1492 and their descendants settled in Ottoman-ruled Safed in the Galilee, which became a major sixteenth-century centre of Kabbalah and halakha. The connection between the expulsion and the flowering of Safed is reported as historical background.

Joseph Karo, the halakhist and author of the Shulchan Arukh who was born in Iberia around the time of the expulsion and later settled in Safed, is one of the figures whose career belongs to the Sephardic diaspora that the expulsion produced. Reported as historical connection, not evaluated.
The expulsion scattered Sephardic Jewry (from Sefarad, Iberia) across North Africa, Italy, and above all the Ottoman Empire, producing the enduring Sephardic diaspora.
The expulsion of 1492 is commonly treated in the historiographical debate over convivencia as a closing point of medieval coexistence among Christians, Muslims, and Jews in Iberia.

Compares the question, not the answer, per neutrality principle #10. Both are expulsions of a religious minority ordered by the Spanish Crown on grounds that included protecting the Catholic faith, and historians of the Moriscos draw the comparison: Rafael Benítez Sánchez-Blanco, writing on the fate of the expelled Moriscos as communities, observes that 'la comparación con los judíos expulsados y con los judeoconversos puede ser ilustrativa'. They differ in whom they targeted and what they left open: the decree of 1492 expelled professing Jews and left baptism as the alternative to exile, whereas the decrees of 1609-1614 expelled baptized Christians of Muslim descent, whom the royal letter treated as apostates, with exemptions only for limited categories such as those judged to live as Christians.
The Alhambra Decree was signed at Granada on 31 March 1492, less than three months after the Nasrid capital was surrendered to Ferdinand and Isabella on 2 January 1492.

Granada'); the stated rationale ('there were some wicked Christians who Judaized and apostatized from our holy Catholic faith, the great cause of which was interaction between the Jews and these Christians'; that Jews would 'subvert and ... steal faithful Christians from our holy Catholic faith'); the command ('resolve to order the said Jews and Jewesses of our kingdoms to depart and never to return'); the deadline ('by the end of the month of July'); the penalty ('the penalty of death and the confiscation of all their possessions'); the export ban ('they do not export gold or silver or coined money'); and the dating ('Given in our city of Granada, the XXXI day of the month of March ... one thousand four hundred and ninety-two years').

sources.citation: Kamen, Henry. "The Mediterranean and the Expulsion of Spanish Jews in 1492." Past & Present 119, no. 1 (1988): 30-55. A peer-reviewed study of the expulsion and its demographic and economic dimensions, revising older estimates of the number expelled sharply downward (Kamen argues for a Jewish population on the order of tens of thousands rather than the hundreds of thousands of older accounts). The academic-history lens on the scale of the expulsion; verified to exist and be on-topic (Oxford Academic / Past & Present record), not read line-by-line.

Netanyahu, Benzion. The Origins of the Inquisition in Fifteenth Century Spain. New York: Random House, 1995. A major, and much-debated, study of the conversos (New Christians) and the origins of the Spanish Inquisition, arguing that the conversos were largely sincere Christians persecuted on grounds that shaded into a doctrine of 'purity of blood' (limpieza de sangre). Cited for the converso / marrano aftermath that frames the 1492 expulsion, with its central thesis noted as a contested scholarly position rather than adopted. Verified to exist and be on-topic (publisher and library records), not read line-by-line.
